evidence.support_text: All 16 subjects reported intense stinging and burning of the lips, cheeks and tongue within 30 s of rinsing with 15 ml of commercial mouthwash containing 0.18% cinnamaldehyde.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 20 mg cinnamic aldehyde in 4 g peanut butter, single oral dose
evidence.support_text: In an uncontrolled oral challenge test, subjects ingested 20 mg of cinnamic aldehyde in 4 g of peanut butter. No change was observed at the patch test sites, indicating no systemic flare of skin sensitization.

evidence.assay_type: protein binding in human skin homogenates
evidence.experimental_conditions: human skin homogenates
evidence.support_text: A recent study investigating the binding of cinnamaldehyde to human skin homogenates showed that this moderate sensitizer was bound to a broad range of proteins in the sample, and there did not appear to be any specific targeting to any particular proteins.

evidence.experimental_conditions: In vitro human skin absorption/metabolism study (Smith et al., 2000, 2001)
evidence.support_text: Activating metabolism of cinnamic alcohol to cinnamaldehyde occurred on the skin surface only; no free cinnamaldehyde derived from cinnamic alcohol was found within the skin, suggesting any formed cinnamaldehyde had bound to skin proteins.

evidence.assay_type: GC-MS analysis of urinary mercapturic acids
evidence.experimental_conditions: Human volunteers; single oral dose 50 mg (0.7 mg/kg) cinnamaldehyde in gelatin capsule; urine collected up to 5 h after ingestion; GC-MS with selective ion monitoring
evidence.support_text: In a human study, six healthy volunteers received a single oral dose of 50 mg cinnamaldehyde. Two mercapturic acid metabolites, N-acetyl-S-(1-phenyl-3-hydroxypropyl)cysteine and N-acetyl-S-(1-phenyl-3-carboxypropyl)cysteine (in an average ratio of 11:1), were detected in urine by GC-MS, indicating in vivo conjugation of cinnamaldehyde with glutathione.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Rat, intraperitoneal administration of comparable doses of methyl acrylate (0.14 mM/kg)
evidence.support_text: In contrast to MMA, administration of comparable doses of methyl acrylate resulted in demonstrable thioether excretion both with and without carboxylesterase inhibition (source Delbressine et al., 1981).
